items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Symbols and subscript numbers that show the elements in a substance and the ratio of their atoms or ions"?
items.answer: chemical formula
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of chemical formula.

items.stem: "Burning a candle destroys matter because the candle gets smaller." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air; mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air; mass is conserved. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Burning a candle destroys matter because the candle gets smaller." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air; mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air; mass is conserved. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In the balanced equation CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, count the number of atoms of each element on the right-hand side, and explain why it must equal the number on the other side.
items.answer: C: 1, O: 4, H: 4; atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed
items.markingKey: 1-2 counts (C: 1, O: 4, H: 4), multiplying subscripts by coefficients; 1 conservation of atoms/mass.

items.stem: Yusuf plans to investigate how the mass of magnesium burned affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed, to test the law of conservation of mass. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: heating until constant mass; lid lifted briefly to let air in; the same balance; clean ribbon (sanded)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: heating until constant mass – ensures all magnesium has reacted; lid lifted briefly to let air in – oxygen is needed but smoke (MgO) must not escape; the same balance – consistent readings; clean ribbon (sanded) – oxide coating adds mass. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that burning a candle destroys matter because the candle gets smaller. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air; mass is conserved.
items.markingKey: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air; mass is conserved. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Rafael plans an investigation into how the mass of magnesium burned affects the mass of magnesium oxide formed, to test the law of conservation of mass. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass of magnesium ribbon (0.10-0.60 g, weighed to 0.01 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: "Word equations are just as useful as balanced symbol equations." Discuss.
items.answer: Word equations are useful for identification, but balanced symbol equations are needed for quantitative chemistry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: easier to read for non-chemists; name the substances clearly. Arguments against: do not show the ratio of particles reacting; cannot be used to calculate masses of reactants and products; do not show conservation of atoms. Supported judgement: Word equations are useful for identification, but balanced symbol equations are needed for quantitative chemistry. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "law of conservation of mass"?
options: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
In a chemical reaction no atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in a formula
A reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances, often by heating (thermal decomposition)
items.answer: In a chemical reaction no atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products
items.markingKey: B. "law of conservation of mass" is in a chemical reaction no atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.

items.stem: Explain why brackets are needed in the formula Mg(OH)₂.
items.answer: The subscript 2 applies to the whole hydroxide ion (one O and one H); without brackets MgOH₂ would mean one O and two H.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The subscript 2 applies to the whole hydroxide ion (one O and one H); without brackets MgOH₂ would mean one O and two H. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a subscript and a coefficient.
items.answer: A coefficient (large number in front) shows how many formula units take part; a subscript (small number) shows how many atoms of an element are in one formula unit and cannot be changed when balancing.
items.markingKey: A coefficient (large number in front) shows how many formula units take part; a subscript (small number) shows how many atoms of an element are in one formula unit and cannot be changed when balancing. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Balance the equation: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
items.answer: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
items.markingKey: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 1 correct coefficients for each side; 1 check: atoms of each element equal on both sides (H 4, O 2).

items.stem:
Ana heated different masses of magnesium ribbon in a lidded crucible until there was no further change and weighed the magnesium oxide formed.

Mass of magnesium / g | Mass of magnesium oxide / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.12 | 0.18 | 0.18 | 0.18
0.24 | 0.36 | 0.37 | 0.36
0.36 | 0.52 | 0.53 | 0.53
0.48 | 0.97 | 0.73 | 0.74
0.6 | 0.91 | 0.92 | 0.87

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean mass of magnesium oxide at 0.48 g, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 0.97 g (trial 1 at 0.48 g); mean = 0.73 g
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (0.97) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 0.73 g.

items.stem: Diego writes: "To balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, change the formula of water to H₂O₂." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Changing the formula changes the substance; put coefficients in front instead: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
items.markingKey: Changing the formula changes the substance; put coefficients in front instead: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that word equations are just as useful as balanced symbol equations?
items.answer: Word equations are useful for identification, but balanced symbol equations are needed for quantitative chemistry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: easier to read for non-chemists; name the substances clearly. Arguments against: do not show the ratio of particles reacting; cannot be used to calculate masses of reactants and products; do not show conservation of atoms. Supported judgement: Word equations are useful for identification, but balanced symbol equations are needed for quantitative chemistry. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "precipitation reaction"?
options: A reaction between two solutions that forms an insoluble solid (precipitate)
A symbol equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in a formula
The percentage of the mass of a compound that is due to each element
items.answer: A reaction between two solutions that forms an insoluble solid (precipitate)
items.markingKey: A. "precipitation reaction" is a reaction between two solutions that forms an insoluble solid (precipitate).

items.stem: Distinguish between a decomposition reaction and a synthesis reaction.
items.answer: Synthesis combines two or more substances into one product; decomposition breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances.
items.markingKey: Synthesis combines two or more substances into one product; decomposition breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the reaction of magnesium with oxygen is described as a synthesis reaction.
items.answer: Two elements combine to form a single new compound, magnesium oxide.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Two elements combine to form a single new compound, magnesium oxide. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Classify the reaction Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ as synthesis, decomposition, displacement, neutralisation, precipitation or combustion, and justify your choice.
items.answer: displacement
items.markingKey: 1 displacement; 1 justification from the equation (e.g. number of reactants/products, element replacing another, acid + base, insoluble product, burning in oxygen).

items.stem:
Ingrid heated different masses of calcium carbonate strongly in a crucible (thermal decomposition) and measured the mass lost.

Mass of calcium carbonate / g | Mass lost / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1.0 | 0.46 | 0.45 | 0.44
2.0 | 0.91 | 0.89 | 0.91
3.0 | 1.39 | 1.36 | 1.38
4.0 | 1.83 | 1.78 | 1.78
5.0 | 2.31 | 2.26 | 2.27

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The mass lost increases in proportion to the mass of calcium carbonate heated (about 44% of the starting mass). CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); the carbon dioxide gas escapes, and 100 g of CaCO₃ releases 44 g of CO₂.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The mass lost increases in proportion to the mass of calcium carbonate heated (about 44% of the starting mass).; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); the carbon dioxide gas escapes, and 100 g of CaCO₃ releases 44 g of CO₂.

items.stem: Classify each reaction and justify: (i) 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g); (ii) Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s); (iii) 4Fe(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Fe₂O₃(s). Then explain which of the three would show a mass decrease in an open beaker.
items.answer: (i) decomposition – one reactant, two products; (ii) displacement – zinc replaces copper; (iii) synthesis/oxidation – two elements form one compound. (i) shows a mass decrease because oxygen gas escapes; (iii) would gain mass from oxygen in air.
items.markingKey: (i) decomposition – one reactant, two products; (ii) displacement – zinc replaces copper; (iii) synthesis/oxidation – two elements form one compound. (i) shows a mass decrease because oxygen gas escapes; (iii) would gain mass from oxygen in air.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "displacement reaction"?
options: A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound
A substance present at the start of a reaction that is used up
A reaction between two solutions that forms an insoluble solid (precipitate)
The gain of oxygen (or the loss of electrons) by a substance
items.answer: A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound
items.markingKey: A. "displacement reaction" is a reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Displacement reactions only happen between metals and acids." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Displacement happens whenever a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound, e.g. metals in salt solutions or halogens in halide solutions.
items.markingKey: Displacement happens whenever a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound, e.g. metals in salt solutions or halogens in halide solutions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a synthesis reaction and a decomposition reaction.
items.answer: Synthesis combines two or more substances into one product; decomposition breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances.
items.markingKey: Synthesis combines two or more substances into one product; decomposition breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that water in an equation should always be written H₂O(aq). Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Pure water is a liquid, H₂O(l); (aq) means dissolved in water.
items.markingKey: Pure water is a liquid, H₂O(l); (aq) means dissolved in water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using lime kilns as an example, explain thermal decomposition.
items.answer: For thousands of years limestone (CaCO₃) has been heated in kilns to make quicklime (CaO) for mortar and agriculture. Heat breaks calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
items.markingKey: Context (For thousands of years limestone (CaCO₃) has been heated in kilns to make quicklime (CaO) for mortar and agriculture.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Heat breaks calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to thermal decomposition.

items.stem: Rafael plans an investigation into how the mass of copper(II) carbonate heated affects the mass of carbon dioxide given off during thermal decomposition. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass of copper(II) carbonate (1.0-5.0 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which metal is the most reactive?
items.answer: Potassium
items.markingKey: A. K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.

items.stem: Explain the difference between oxidation and reduction.
items.answer: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they always happen together (redox).
items.markingKey: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they always happen together (redox). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between reduction and oxidation.
items.answer: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they always happen together (redox).
items.markingKey: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they always happen together (redox). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which sacrificial zinc blocks on ships’ hulls shows relative reactivity of metals.
items.answer: Blocks of zinc are bolted onto steel hulls and corrode away instead of the steel. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference, protecting the iron.
items.markingKey: Context (Blocks of zinc are bolted onto steel hulls and corrode away instead of the steel.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference, protecting the iron. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to relative reactivity of metals.

items.stem: Sana places a piece of zinc into iron(II) sulfate solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs, explain your prediction and describe what would be observed.
items.answer: Yes – zinc is more reactive than iron, so it displaces iron: a coating of dark grey iron forms on the zinc and the pale green colour fades; the mixture warms slightly.
items.markingKey: 1 reaction occurs; 1 zinc above iron in the reactivity series; 1 observation: dark grey iron deposited, pale green solution fades.

items.stem: Rafael investigated how the position of a metal in the reactivity series affects the temperature rise when it is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. The method had this weakness: a glass beaker without a lid was used. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid to reduce heat loss
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid to reduce heat loss

items.stem: Define the term "reduction".
items.answer: The loss of oxygen (or the gain of electrons) by a substance
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the loss of oxygen (or the gain of electrons) by a substance. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that copper displaces zinc from zinc sulfate solution because copper is a metal too. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Copper is less reactive than zinc so no reaction occurs; zinc would displace copper.
items.markingKey: Copper is less reactive than zinc so no reaction occurs; zinc would displace copper. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why aluminium is very reactive but aluminium window frames do not corrode.
items.answer: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that sticks to the surface and stops further reaction.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that sticks to the surface and stops further reaction. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia plans to investigate how the position of a metal in the reactivity series affects the temperature rise when it is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: mass and particle size of metal (1.0 g powder); volume and concentration of copper(II) sulfate; insulation of the cup; starting temperature
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: mass and particle size of metal (1.0 g powder) – more surface area reacts faster and more metal releases more energy; volume and concentration of copper(II) sulfate – more copper ions give more reaction; insulation of the cup – reduces heat loss; starting temperature – affects heat loss to surroundings. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that phytomining (using plants to extract metals such as nickel or copper from low-grade soil) should replace traditional mining.
items.answer: It is a useful supplement for low-grade ores and land remediation but cannot replace mining at current demand.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: can recover metal from waste land and low-grade ores; cleans up contaminated land; less landscape damage. Arguments against: very slow (years per harvest); yields are small compared with demand; the plants must still be burned and the metal extracted by electrolysis or displacement. Supported judgement: It is a useful supplement for low-grade ores and land remediation but cannot replace mining at current demand. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Extracting metals by electrolysis is too expensive and should be replaced by recycling." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Recycling should be maximised, but electrolysis remains necessary; its impact depends on the energy source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: electrolysis uses huge amounts of electricity (aluminium smelting); recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy. Arguments against: recycling cannot meet all demand as consumption grows; electrolysis powered by hydroelectricity (e.g. Iceland, Norway) has low emissions; some metals cannot be extracted any other way. Supported judgement: Recycling should be maximised, but electrolysis remains necessary; its impact depends on the energy source. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "percentage composition by mass".
items.answer: The percentage of the mass of a compound that is due to each element
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the percentage of the mass of a compound that is due to each element. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Kenji calculates the Mᵣ of urea, CO(NH₂)₂, as 64. Explain the mistake and give the correct value.
items.answer: The subscript after the bracket multiplies every atom inside the bracket; correct Mᵣ = 60.
items.markingKey: 1 the number outside the bracket applies to all atoms in the bracket (only the last atom was multiplied); 1 correct Mᵣ = 60.

items.stem: "The percentage of carbon in methane (CH₄) is 20% because carbon is 1 of 5 atoms." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Percentage by mass uses relative atomic masses: 12/16 × 100 = 75%.
items.markingKey: Percentage by mass uses relative atomic masses: 12/16 × 100 = 75%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Aiko heated different masses of copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃, until it fully decomposed to copper(II) oxide, CuO, and weighed the residue. (Aᵣ: Cu = 63.5, C = 12, O = 16)

Mass of CuCO₃ / g | Mass of CuO / g: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1.24 | 0.86 | 0.87 | 0.87
2.47 | 1.81 | 1.73 | 1.75
3.71 | 2.62 | 2.74 | 2.72
4.94 | 3.44 | 3.66 | 3.44
6.18 | 4.33 | 4.54 | 4.57

Calculate the mean mass of cuo when the mass of cuco₃ was 4.94 g.
items.markingKey: M1 (3.44 + 3.66 + 3.44) ÷ 3; A1 3.51 g (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Using choosing nitrogen fertilisers in Kenyan smallholder farms as an example, explain percentage composition.
items.answer: Urea, CO(NH₂)₂, contains 46.7% nitrogen, while ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, contains 35%; urea is often cheaper per kg of nitrogen. Calculating %N lets farmers compare how much nitrogen each fertiliser delivers per kilogram.
items.markingKey: Context (Urea, CO(NH₂)₂, contains 46.7% nitrogen, while ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, contains 35%; urea is often cheaper per kg of nitrogen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Calculating %N lets farmers compare how much nitrogen each fertiliser delivers per kilogram. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to percentage composition.

items.stem: A farmer can buy ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) at US$350 per tonne or urea (CO(NH₂)₂) at US$420 per tonne. (Aᵣ: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32, K = 39, C = 12) (a) Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in each. (b) Calculate the cost of 1 kg of nitrogen from each fertiliser. (c) Recommend which to buy and give one other factor the farmer should consider.
items.answer: (a) ammonium nitrate 35.0%, urea 46.7% (b) ammonium nitrate US$1.00/kg N, urea US$0.90/kg N (c) urea; also consider solubility, losses to air/water, other nutrients (S, K), soil pH
items.markingKey: (a) M1 Mᵣ values 80, 60; A1 35.0% and 46.7%. (b) M1 kg N per tonne; A1 1.00 and 0.90. (c) 1 urea (cheaper per kg N); 1 valid other factor.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound"?
items.answer: empirical formula
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of empirical formula.

items.stem: Explain why relative formula mass has no units.
items.answer: It compares the mass of a formula unit with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so it is a ratio.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It compares the mass of a formula unit with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so it is a ratio. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in water, H₂O. (Aᵣ: H = 1, O = 16)
Alessia writes: "The Mᵣ of Ca(OH)₂ is 40 + 16 + 1 × 2 = 58." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The 2 applies to both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74.
items.markingKey: The 2 applies to both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, to compare with the value calculated from the formula MgO. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Burn weighed masses of magnesium (0.2-0.6 g) in a lidded crucible to constant mass; calculate % Mg for each; calculate the mean and compare with 60%; identify systematic errors (e.g. incomplete reaction gives a value above 60%).
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (do not look directly at burning magnesium; use tongs). Model: Burn weighed masses of magnesium (0.2-0.6 g) in a lidded crucible to constant mass; calculate % Mg for each; calculate the mean and compare with 60%; identify systematic errors (e.g. incomplete reaction gives a value above 60%).

items.stem: Why must chemical equations be balanced?
options: To show the reaction is fast
Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction
items.answer: Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction
items.markingKey: D. Mass is conserved.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "synthesis reaction".
items.answer: A reaction in which two or more substances combine to form one product, e.g. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form one product, e.g. 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extraction of the metal economic"?
items.answer: ore
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of ore.

items.stem: Explain the difference between relative formula mass and relative atomic mass.
items.answer: Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is for one element (weighted mean of its isotopes); relative formula mass (Mᵣ) is the sum of the Aᵣ values of all the atoms in a formula.
items.markingKey: Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ) is for one element (weighted mean of its isotopes); relative formula mass (Mᵣ) is the sum of the Aᵣ values of all the atoms in a formula. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why you must not change the small subscript numbers in formulae when balancing an equation.
items.answer: Changing a subscript changes the substance itself (e.g. H₂O to H₂O₂); only the large coefficients in front of formulae may be changed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Changing a subscript changes the substance itself (e.g. H₂O to H₂O₂); only the large coefficients in front of formulae may be changed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Water in an equation should always be written H₂O(aq)." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Pure water is a liquid, H₂O(l); (aq) means dissolved in water.
items.markingKey: Pure water is a liquid, H₂O(l); (aq) means dissolved in water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between reduction and oxidation.
items.answer: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they always happen together (redox).
items.markingKey: Oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; they always happen together (redox). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why percentage composition is useful to farmers choosing a fertiliser.
items.answer: It shows the percentage of nitrogen (or other nutrient) in the fertiliser, so farmers can compare which supplies the most nutrient per kilogram for the money.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows the percentage of nitrogen (or other nutrient) in the fertiliser, so farmers can compare which supplies the most nutrient per kilogram for the money. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the total mass stays the same when silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution in a sealed flask, even though a solid forms.
items.answer: The atoms in the reactants are rearranged into the products (silver chloride precipitate and sodium nitrate solution); no atoms enter or leave the closed flask, so the mass is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The atoms in the reactants are rearranged into the products (silver chloride precipitate and sodium nitrate solution); no atoms enter or leave the closed flask, so the mass is unchanged. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe lime kilns and explain what it reveals about thermal decomposition.
items.answer: For thousands of years limestone (CaCO₃) has been heated in kilns to make quicklime (CaO) for mortar and agriculture. Heat breaks calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
items.markingKey: Context (For thousands of years limestone (CaCO₃) has been heated in kilns to make quicklime (CaO) for mortar and agriculture.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Heat breaks calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to thermal decomposition.

items.stem:
Isabel added 1.0 g of powdered metal to 25 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution and recorded the maximum temperature rise. Metals were placed in order of their position in the reactivity series (1 = magnesium, 2 = zinc, 3 = iron, 4 = lead).

Metal / position | Temperature rise / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 31.7 | 30.7 | 32.0
2 | 13.5 | 13.0 | 13.8
3 | 7.8 | 7.6 | 7.8
4 | 2.1 | 2.2 | 2.3

Calculate the mean temperature rise when the metal was 1 position.
items.markingKey: M1 (31.7 + 30.7 + 32.0) ÷ 3; A1 31.47 °C (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Outline one way in which choosing nitrogen fertilisers in Kenyan smallholder farms shows percentage composition.
items.answer: Urea, CO(NH₂)₂, contains 46.7% nitrogen, while ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, contains 35%; urea is often cheaper per kg of nitrogen. Calculating %N lets farmers compare how much nitrogen each fertiliser delivers per kilogram.
items.markingKey: Context (Urea, CO(NH₂)₂, contains 46.7% nitrogen, while ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, contains 35%; urea is often cheaper per kg of nitrogen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Calculating %N lets farmers compare how much nitrogen each fertiliser delivers per kilogram. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to percentage composition.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "In 2H₂O there are 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The coefficient multiplies the whole formula: 2H₂O contains 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms.
items.markingKey: The coefficient multiplies the whole formula: 2H₂O contains 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Hana is investigating how the mass of copper(II) carbonate heated affects the mass of carbon dioxide given off during thermal decomposition. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: mass of copper(II) carbonate (1.0-5.0 g)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mass of copper(II) carbonate (1.0-5.0 g) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Mei writes: "Copper displaces zinc from zinc sulfate solution because copper is a metal too." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Copper is less reactive than zinc so no reaction occurs; zinc would displace copper.
items.markingKey: Copper is less reactive than zinc so no reaction occurs; zinc would displace copper. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into the percentage by mass of magnesium in magnesium oxide, to compare with the value calculated from the formula MgO, explain why purity of ribbon (sanded) must be kept the same in every trial.
items.answer: oxide layer changes mass
items.markingKey: 1 mark: purity of ribbon (sanded) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: oxide layer changes mass. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that word equations are just as useful as balanced symbol equations.
items.answer: Word equations are useful for identification, but balanced symbol equations are needed for quantitative chemistry.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: easier to read for non-chemists; name the substances clearly. Arguments against: do not show the ratio of particles reacting; cannot be used to calculate masses of reactants and products; do not show conservation of atoms. Supported judgement: Word equations are useful for identification, but balanced symbol equations are needed for quantitative chemistry.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that cement production, which depends on decomposing limestone, should be heavily taxed because of its carbon dioxide emissions.
items.answer: A carbon price is justified, but should be combined with support for new technologies and developing economies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cement causes about 8% of global CO₂ emissions, from decomposition of CaCO₃ and fuel burning; tax encourages low-carbon alternatives and carbon capture. Arguments against: cement is essential for housing and infrastructure, especially in developing countries; costs passed to consumers; alternatives are not yet available at scale. Supported judgement: A carbon price is justified, but should be combined with support for new technologies and developing economies. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem:
Three metals, X, Y and Z, were placed in solutions of each other’s salts. Results:
Y in a solution of a Z salt: reaction
Z in a solution of a X salt: no reaction
Z in a solution of a Y salt: no reaction
X in a solution of a Y salt: no reaction
X in a solution of a Z salt: reaction
Y in a solution of a X salt: reaction
(a) Deduce the order of reactivity of X, Y and Z, most reactive first. (b) Explain your reasoning. (c) Suggest how the reliability of the conclusion could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Y > X > Z (b) the most reactive metal displaces both others; the least reactive displaces neither (c) repeat with fresh, cleaned metal samples and the same concentration of solutions, or measure temperature rise
items.markingKey: (a) 2 for Y > X > Z (1 if one pair swapped). (b) 1 a metal displaces only metals below it; 1 counts of reactions used. (c) 1 valid improvement (clean metal surfaces, equal concentrations, repeats, measure temperature change).

items.stem: "Fertilisers with the highest percentage of nitrogen are always the best choice." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: High %N is useful but the best choice also depends on crop, soil, cost and environmental losses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: supply more nitrogen per kg, cheaper to transport; less needed per field. Arguments against: some forms (urea) lose nitrogen as ammonia gas if not incorporated; solubility and release rate matter; excess nitrogen causes eutrophication of rivers and lakes. Supported judgement: High %N is useful but the best choice also depends on crop, soil, cost and environmental losses. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "chemical formula".
items.answer: Symbols and subscript numbers that show the elements in a substance and the ratio of their atoms or ions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: symbols and subscript numbers that show the elements in a substance and the ratio of their atoms or ions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances, often by heating (thermal decomposition)"?
items.answer: decomposition reaction
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of decomposition reaction.

items.stem: Which metal can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon?
items.answer: Iron
items.markingKey: Iron. Carbon is more reactive than iron but less reactive than Al, Mg and Na.

items.stem: "The Mᵣ of Ca(OH)₂ is 40 + 16 + 1 × 2 = 58." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The 2 applies to both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74.
items.markingKey: The 2 applies to both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia writes the equation 2C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Explain why this equation is not balanced and write the correct balanced equation.
items.answer: Atoms of C, H are not equal on both sides; correct: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
items.markingKey: 1 counts atoms on each side and identifies the unequal element(s): C, H; 1 atoms cannot be created or destroyed; 1 correct equation C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.

items.stem: Distinguish between a synthesis reaction and a decomposition reaction.
items.answer: Synthesis combines two or more substances into one product; decomposition breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances.
items.markingKey: Synthesis combines two or more substances into one product; decomposition breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why gold is found as the uncombined metal in the Earth’s crust.
items.answer: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not readily react with oxygen, water or other substances and stays as the element.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not readily react with oxygen, water or other substances and stays as the element. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the percentage composition of a compound can be used to identify which of two possible compounds a sample is.
items.answer: Each compound has a fixed composition; analysing the sample’s mass of each element and comparing with the calculated percentages shows which formula matches.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each compound has a fixed composition; analysing the sample’s mass of each element and comparing with the calculated percentages shows which formula matches. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the formula of aluminium oxide is Al₂O₃.
items.answer: Al forms Al³⁺ and O forms O²⁻; the lowest common multiple of the charges is 6, so 2 Al³⁺ (+6) balance 3 O²⁻ (−6).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Al forms Al³⁺ and O forms O²⁻; the lowest common multiple of the charges is 6, so 2 Al³⁺ (+6) balance 3 O²⁻ (−6). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Add state symbols to this equation for a reaction carried out at room temperature (water as solvent where needed): CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
items.answer: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
items.markingKey: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). 1 mark per two correct state symbols (max 3). Note: water as a liquid product is (l); dissolved ionic salts and acids are (aq); insoluble salts/metals/oxides (s).

items.stem: With reference to sacrificial zinc blocks on ships’ hulls, explain how it illustrates relative reactivity of metals.
items.answer: Blocks of zinc are bolted onto steel hulls and corrode away instead of the steel. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference, protecting the iron.
items.markingKey: Context (Blocks of zinc are bolted onto steel hulls and corrode away instead of the steel.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons (is oxidised) in preference, protecting the iron. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to relative reactivity of metals.

items.stem: A student claims that the Mᵣ of Ca(OH)₂ is 40 + 16 + 1 × 2 = 58. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The 2 applies to both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74.
items.markingKey: The 2 applies to both O and H: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "To balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, change the formula of water to H₂O₂." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Changing the formula changes the substance; put coefficients in front instead: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
items.markingKey: Changing the formula changes the substance; put coefficients in front instead: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo wants to find out how the mass of copper(II) carbonate heated affects the mass of carbon dioxide given off during thermal decomposition. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does mass of copper(II) carbonate affect mass of CO₂ lost?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (mass of copper(II) carbonate (1.0-5.0 g)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (mass of CO₂ lost – mass of tube and contents before and after heating to constant mass) in a question form.

items.stem: Briefly describe the blast furnace in steelworks (e.g. in Jamshedpur, India) and explain what it reveals about the reactivity series and extraction.
items.answer: Iron ore (Fe₂O₃) is heated with coke; carbon monoxide reduces the ore to molten iron. Carbon is above iron in the reactivity series, so it can remove oxygen from iron oxide.
items.markingKey: Context (Iron ore (Fe₂O₃) is heated with coke; carbon monoxide reduces the ore to molten iron.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Carbon is above iron in the reactivity series, so it can remove oxygen from iron oxide. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the reactivity series and extraction.

items.stem: The equation for burning magnesium ribbon in a crucible is 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. (Aᵣ: Mg = 24, O = 16) (a) Calculate the Mᵣ of Mg and of MgO. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of MgO that can be made from 10 g of Mg. (c) Explain how this calculation depends on the law of conservation of mass.
items.answer: (a) 24 and 40 (b) 16.7 g (c) atoms are conserved, so the balanced equation fixes the ratio of masses

items.stem: "Extracting metals by electrolysis is too expensive and should be replaced by recycling." Discuss.
items.answer: Recycling should be maximised, but electrolysis remains necessary; its impact depends on the energy source.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: electrolysis uses huge amounts of electricity (aluminium smelting); recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy. Arguments against: recycling cannot meet all demand as consumption grows; electrolysis powered by hydroelectricity (e.g. Iceland, Norway) has low emissions; some metals cannot be extracted any other way. items.stem: A farmer can buy potassium nitrate (KNO₃) at US$350 per tonne or urea (CO(NH₂)₂) at US$380 per tonne. (Aᵣ: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32, K = 39, C = 12) (a) Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in each. (b) Calculate the cost of 1 kg of nitrogen from each fertiliser. (c) Recommend which to buy and give one other factor the farmer should consider.
items.answer: (a) potassium nitrate 13.9%, urea 46.7% (b) potassium nitrate US$2.52/kg N, urea US$0.81/kg N (c) urea; also consider solubility, losses to air/water, other nutrients (S, K), soil pH
items.markingKey: (a) M1 Mᵣ values 101, 60; A1 13.9% and 46.7%. (b) M1 kg N per tonne; A1 2.52 and 0.81. (c) 1 urea (cheaper per kg N); 1 valid other factor.
